claims.title: Media exposure causes eating disorders in children and adolescents
claims.institution: PubMed Central / National Institutes of Health
claims.summary: Media content — particularly advertising — promotes unrealistic body ideals in children and adolescents. The study documents the causal link between media exposure and the development of eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa.
claims.finding: Body dissatisfaction in children and adolescents is directly associated with media consumption and leads to reduced quality of life, deteriorated mood, and unhealthy eating habits. Advertising that portrays unrealistic ideals of thinness is a primary trigger.

claims.title: Advertising causes body shame, depression, and anxiety disorders in adolescents
claims.summary: Self-objectification through advertising exposure is linked to body shame, depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. The study analyzes the psychological mechanisms through which advertising content damages the self-image of young people.
claims.finding: Exposure to beauty and diet content from advertising accelerates the development of eating disorders. A report by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (2023) found that algorithmically delivered content worsened body image anxiety in 70% of adolescents. Outdoor advertising permanently transports the same images into public space.

claims.title: Attention-forcing advertising tactics manipulate behavior despite perceived manipulation
claims.summary: Advertising tactics designed to compel attention cause consumers to perceive manipulative intent — thereby reducing advertising effectiveness, brand attitude, and purchase intent. Yet studies show that even recognized manipulation still influences purchasing behavior.
claims.finding: When advertising is perceived as manipulative, attitudes toward the advertisement, attitudes toward the brand, and purchase intent all decline significantly. This demonstrates that outdoor advertising is deliberately designed to compel attention — and in doing so violates the cognitive autonomy of passers-by.

claims.title: Subliminal messages influence decisions below the threshold of consciousness over the long term
claims.summary: Neuroscientific research confirms that subliminal messages can influence decisions under certain conditions — particularly when they align with existing needs or desires. These effects are demonstrable over the long term.
claims.finding: Subliminal messages can steer decisions in a particular direction without the affected person noticing. Advertising deliberately exploits these mechanisms: brief image sequences, subliminal messages, and emotional conditioning in outdoor advertising influence behavior below the threshold of conscious perception.

claims.title: Subliminal advertising demonstrably influences purchasing behavior
claims.summary: Empirical study examining the influence of subliminal advertising on purchasing behavior. Non-marketing experts and young consumers are particularly susceptible to unconscious influence through advertising messages.
claims.finding: Subliminal advertising measurably influences purchasing behavior, especially among groups without media literacy training. Children and adolescents, as well as individuals without marketing knowledge, are most severely affected.

claims.title: Creative outdoor advertising deliberately manipulates unconscious cognitive processing
claims.summary: Field studies on outdoor advertising show that creativity in advertising visuals is deliberately deployed to hijack involuntary attention and create brand memory through context-dependent memory mechanisms.
claims.finding: Outdoor advertising deliberately exploits the orienting response mechanism (unconscious attentional orientation toward novel stimuli), context-dependent memory formation, and cognitive fluency. Creative advertising thereby overcomes a cognitive "attention threshold" — meaning it is designed so as to compel involuntary attention.

claims.title: Digital billboards consume 30 times more energy than an average US household
claims.summary: DarkSky International, the leading independent organization for light pollution research, documents the enormous energy consumption of digital billboards and their effects on light pollution and ecosystems.
claims.finding: Digital billboards consume 30 times more energy than an average American household. Electronic Message Centers (EMCs) emit light in all directions (non-directional), can be 10 times brighter than traditional billboards at night, and contribute to global light pollution, which is increasing by 6% annually. 88% of Europe and 50% of the USA are already experiencing perpetual artificial twilight.

claims.title: Digital advertising emits 7.2 million tonnes of CO₂ per year — more than the entire aviation industry
claims.institution: Journal of Marketing Communications, Taylor & Francis
claims.summary: Academic analysis (Journal of Marketing Communications) and corroborating data from The Drum show: the digital advertising industry emits 7.2 million tonnes of CO₂ per year — more than the entire aviation industry. DOOH contributes to this through both direct energy consumption (screens, servers) and indirect emissions generated by consumption incentives.
claims.finding: The digital advertising industry emits 7.2 million tonnes of CO₂ per year — equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of 1.4 million US households and an estimated 1.7% of global greenhouse gas emissions by 2025 (aviation: 1.9%). A single digital advertising campaign generates approximately 70 tonnes of CO₂e — the annual emissions of 7 people. In addition, there are massive indirect emissions: online advertising accounts for 10–20% of total internet infrastructure energy consumption; DOOH combines both effects.

claims.title: Systematic assessment of the environmental cost of digital advertising campaigns
claims.summary: The first systematic assessment of the environmental costs of digital advertising campaigns using life cycle analyses. Quantifies energy consumption and CO₂ emissions per ad placement.
claims.finding: Digital advertising causes measurable and quantifiable environmental costs that have so far not been taken into account in any regulation. The study provides a methodology for calculating the ecological footprint of advertising campaigns — outdoor advertising with continuously operating screens is particularly cost-intensive.

claims.title: Light pollution from outdoor advertising harms wildlife and disrupts human sleep
claims.summary: Light from digital billboards and illuminated outdoor advertising affects the behavior of nocturnal animals and disrupts biological rhythms in both humans and animals. Global light pollution is increasing by 6% annually.
claims.finding: Artificial light from billboards disrupts the reproduction, foraging, and orientation of nocturnal animals: birds, bats, frogs, and insects become disoriented or are directly harmed. For humans: excessive artificial light at night leads to sleep disorders, endocrine disruptions, and increased cancer risk (melatonin suppression).

claims.title: Visual pollution from advertising lowers quality of life in cities
claims.institution: University College London, The Bartlett School of Planning / Routledge
claims.summary: An empirical comparative study (UK and Brazil) on the negative effects of commercial signage and advertising on the visual quality of urban spaces and the quality of life of residents. Examined from architectural, planning, and psychological perspectives.
claims.finding: Commercial signage and outdoor advertising have demonstrably negative consequences for the visual quality of urban spaces and the well-being of residents. The study establishes that visual overload from advertising acts as an environmental stressor.

claims.title: Outdoor advertising is a measurable source of visual pollution — cities lack a regulatory methodology
claims.institution: International Journal of Geographical Information Science, Taylor & Francis
claims.summary: Development of a methodology for measuring visual pollution caused by outdoor advertising on urban streets, combining intervisibility analysis with public surveys. Demonstrates that over-stimulating advertising is a quantifiable source of visual pollution.
claims.finding: Outdoor advertising is a measurable source of visual pollution on urban streets. Cities lack standardized measurement methods, which makes effective regulation impossible. The study provides, for the first time, a scientific tool for quantifying the problem.

claims.title: Visual pollution causes stress, anxiety, and diminished mental health
claims.summary: A European comparative study on urban visual pollution, published in Nature Scientific Reports. Shows that visual pollution is far more than an aesthetic problem — it acts as an environmental stressor with direct health consequences.
claims.finding: Visual pollution is a significant environmental problem driven by rapid urbanization. It is not merely an aesthetic nuisance, but acts directly on mental health: it contributes to anxiety, stress, and reduced quality of life. Advertising is one of the primary drivers of visual pollution in urban spaces.

claims.title: Advertising privatizes public space without democratic accountability
claims.summary: A critical urban analysis of outdoor advertising as a mechanism for privatizing public space. Examines how advertising imposes a specific "order" on the cityscape and undermines democratic control over public space.
claims.finding: Advertising imposes a particular "spatial order" (Raumordnung) on public space that places commercial interests above public interests. Regulatory mechanisms operating under the label of "public accountability" serve commercial interests in practice. The "advertising city" dispossesses citizens of their shared urban space (urban commons).

claims.title: Systematic review: visual pollution as a growing environmental problem
claims.summary: A systematic literature review on visual pollution as an environmental problem. Identifies research gaps and methodological approaches to measurement and regulation. Published in 2024 in MDPI Land.
claims.finding: Visual pollution is a recognized and growing environmental problem. Research shows consistent negative impacts on well-being and urban quality. Outdoor advertising is one of the primary drivers, yet it is barely captured by urban environmental regulations.

claims.title: Status advertising generates status anxiety and drives households into debt
claims.summary: Review study on the relationship between income inequality, status-driven consumption, and status anxiety. Shows that advertising promoting status symbols directly contributes to household debt and non-sustainable consumption.
claims.finding: Income inequality is associated with higher status-driven consumption and status anxiety. This status anxiety, fuelled by advertising, leads to household debt, spatial inequalities, and non-sustainable consumption behaviour with higher CO₂ emissions.

claims.title: Rising inequality driven by advertising pressure fuels consumer credit
claims.institution: Quantitative Marketing and Economics, Springer Nature
claims.summary: Econometric study on the relationship between rising income inequality and growing consumer debt. Shows that households with smaller income gains take on debt to maintain their consumption relative to wealthier households.
claims.finding: Rising income inequality substantially increases consumer debt. Households with smaller income gains take on debt to emulate the consumption of wealthier groups — a mechanism that advertising deliberately exploits ("Keeping up with the Joneses").

claims.title: Long-term correlation: growing inequality and consumption-driven indebtedness since the 1960s
claims.summary: NBER (National Bureau of Economic Research) working paper documenting the long-term correlation between growing income inequality and consumption patterns in the USA since the 1960s. Analyses how marketing and advertising accelerate status-driven consumption.
claims.finding: Decades of data confirm the relationship between rising inequality and non-sustainable consumption patterns. Advertising and marketing play a central role in accelerating status-driven consumption that perpetuates inequalities.

claims.title: Higher inequality leads to more status consumption — advertising deliberately exploits this mechanism
claims.institution: Wharton School of Business, University of Pennsylvania
claims.summary: Wharton School of Business research study on the effect of income inequality on conspicuous and inconspicuous consumption. Shows that higher inequality leads to more ostentatious (visible) status consumption — precisely what outdoor advertising for high-priced goods incentivises.
claims.finding: Higher inequality increases status-signalling consumption (conspicuous consumption). Advertising for luxury goods and status products in public space deliberately exploits and amplifies this mechanism — it targets all income groups and generates social comparison processes that lead to irrational purchasing decisions.

claims.title: Outdoor food advertising influences adolescents as strongly as TV advertising
claims.summary: Systematic review study on outdoor food advertising: reach, effectiveness, and impacts on eating behavior and health. Published in BMC Public Health, Springer Nature.
claims.finding: Outdoor food advertising is as extensive and effective as digital or TV advertising. Skepticism among adolescents does not protect against its effects. Both young children and older adolescents are susceptible. Evidence shows that advertising influences dietary preferences and consumption patterns.

claims.title: Outdoor food advertising directly correlates with purchasing behavior in adolescents
claims.summary: Canadian cross-sectional study that establishes for the first time a direct correlation between exposure to outdoor food advertising and the actual purchasing behavior of adolescents. Peer-reviewed, published in Oxford Health Promotion International.
claims.finding: The study demonstrates a statistically significant direct correlation between the frequency of exposure to outdoor food advertising and the purchasing behavior of adolescents. More advertising = more purchases of the advertised (predominantly unhealthy) products.

claims.title: 10% more food advertising per neighborhood → 1.05-fold higher risk of overweight
claims.summary: Cross-sectional study quantifying the relationship between the density of food advertising in a neighborhood and the residents' risk of overweight. Published in BMC Public Health.
claims.finding: A higher proportion of food advertising in neighborhoods is associated with increased rates of overweight and obesity. For every 10% increase in the share of food advertising, the risk of overweight rises by a factor of 1.05. The effect is measurable at the neighborhood level and is statistically significant.

claims.title: WHO: voluntary restrictions on food advertising to children are ineffective
claims.summary: WHO guideline and ELENA (e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions) intervention on food marketing to children. The WHO recommends binding legislative measures to protect children from marketing for foods high in saturated fats, trans fats, free sugars, and salt.
claims.finding: Voluntary self-regulatory commitments by the advertising industry are demonstrably ineffective. The WHO calls for binding, state-enforced restrictions — including for outdoor advertising — because otherwise children are left defenseless against aggressive marketing.

claims.title: Harmful marketing kills over 1 million people per year in the US alone
claims.summary: Peer-reviewed study in Prevention Science (Springer) analyzing harmful marketing as an overlooked social determinant of health. Examines 6 industries: tobacco, alcohol, pharmaceuticals, processed foods, firearms, and fossil fuels.
claims.finding: Marketing across 6 industries is causally responsible for disease and death. More than 1 million Americans die annually from the consequences of products promoted through marketing. The study frames harmful marketing as a structural public health determinant — comparable to poverty or lack of education.

claims.title: Global outdoor advertising acts as a driver of cultural homogenization
claims.institution: Asian Journal of Communication, Taylor & Francis
claims.summary: Academic analysis of advertising as a culturally homogenising force in the ASEAN region. Examines how international advertising challenges national cultural projects and spreads Western cultural elements worldwide.
claims.finding: International advertising — particularly for global brands in public space — functions as a global cultural homogenisation force. It spreads a unified Western (primarily American) visual identity and value system across national borders, displacing local cultural ideals.

claims.title: Western advertising displaces local beauty and cultural ideals worldwide
claims.summary: Academic analysis of how global advertising and consumer culture contribute to the emergence of a homogeneous global culture. Specifically examines global brands (Coca-Cola, Apple, McDonald's) and their effect on cultural convergence.
claims.finding: Global brands impose a consistent image and value system across national borders, promoting cultural convergence. Local cultural ideals — including beauty standards — are increasingly aligning with Western norms. Outdoor advertising is the primary channel through which these messages penetrate public space.

claims.title: Global advertising platforms accelerate cultural homogenization and threaten local traditions
claims.summary: Current (2024) analysis of how global advertising platforms and media — including outdoor advertising — contribute to cultural homogenisation and threaten local traditions and diversity.
claims.finding: Global advertising and media platforms contribute measurably to cultural homogenisation. Local traditions and cultural diversity are being displaced by the dominance of global brand messages in public space. This is a currently growing problem.

claims.title: Children's school routes are systematically burdened with harmful product advertising
claims.summary: Study on the distribution of harmful product advertising (alcohol, unhealthy food, gambling) in public space and on school routes. Also analyzes the effectiveness of advertising bans.
claims.finding: Children are systematically exposed to advertising for harmful products on their way to school. Advertising along home-to-school routes reinforces messages through repetition. Neighborhoods with particularly high exposure show elevated health risks. Voluntary bans are ineffective — only mandatory government regulations show measurable impact.

claims.title: Low-income neighborhoods and Communities of Color are disproportionately exposed to harmful outdoor advertising
claims.institution: PubMed / American Journal of Public Health
claims.summary: Environmental justice (the fair distribution of environmental benefits and burdens) study in Los Angeles on the spatial inequality of harmful outdoor advertising (alcohol, tobacco, junk food). Reveals structural racism and class inequality in the placement of outdoor advertising.
claims.finding: Low-income neighborhoods and neighborhoods with a high proportion of people of color bear a disproportionately high burden of harmful outdoor advertising. The distribution is not random but follows patterns that correlate with existing social inequalities — outdoor advertising reinforces and perpetuates these inequalities.

claims.title: 92% of food advertising targeting children in Germany promotes unhealthy products
claims.institution: Universität Hamburg, Fachbereich BWL, im Auftrag von DANK und AOK-Bundesverband
claims.summary: Study by the University of Hamburg, commissioned by the Deutsche Allianz Nichtübertragbare Krankheiten (DANK — German Alliance for Non-Communicable Diseases) and the AOK-Bundesverband (national health insurer federation). Systematically analyzes food advertising directed at children in Germany.
claims.finding: A child between 3 and 13 years of age in Germany sees an average of 15 food advertisements for unhealthy products per day (5 online, 10 on television). 92% of all food advertisements directed at children concern unhealthy products (89% on TV, 98% online).

claims.title: 50% of adolescents in Germany purchased products due to influencer advertising
claims.institution: Fraunhofer-Institut für System- und Innovationsforschung (ISI), Karlsruhe
claims.summary: DFG (Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft — German Research Foundation)-funded FAIR project (Fraunhofer ISI, Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences, University of Mannheim) examining the impact of influencer marketing on adolescents in Germany. Survey of more than 1,000 adolescents.
claims.finding: Approximately 50% of surveyed adolescents had purchased products advertised by influencers. More than half had spent over 50 euros on influencer-promoted products within 6 months. Adolescents are particularly vulnerable due to intensive social media use and less developed advertising literacy.

claims.title: Light pollution from artificial lighting demonstrably causes insect die-off
claims.institution: Leibniz-Institut für Gewässerökologie und Binnenfischerei (IGB), Berlin
claims.summary: Research by the Leibniz-Institut für Gewässerökologie und Binnenfischerei (IGB) (Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries), Berlin, demonstrates a clear causal link between light pollution and the decline of flying insects. Regions with severe insect decline also show high levels of light pollution.
claims.finding: In regions with severe declines in flying insects, levels of light pollution are also high. IGB researchers found strong evidence for a causal relationship. Artificial light at night disrupts the reproduction, foraging, and orientation of insects.

claims.title: Artificial night light alters 1,564 genes in insects — massive physiological damage
claims.summary: Research by the Senckenberg Gesellschaft für Naturforschung (Senckenberg Society for Nature Research), Frankfurt, on the molecular effects of light pollution on insects. For the first time, the extent to which artificial light at night influences the gene expression of insects was demonstrated.
claims.finding: Artificial light at night causes profound changes in the gene expression of insects: 1,564 genes were affected in midge larvae (Chironomidae). The consequences include delayed development, increased oxidative stress, and drastically reduced reproductive capacity. This threatens the entire food chain, as insects form the foundation for birds, fish, and other animals.

claims.title: Light pollution as a cause of insect decline — Bavarian state authority confirms the link
claims.institution: Bayerische Akademie für Naturschutz und Landschaftspflege (ANL Bayern)
claims.summary: A comprehensive analysis by the Bayerische Akademie für Naturschutz und Landschaftspflege (ANL Bayern) (Bavarian Academy for Nature Conservation and Landscape Management) on light pollution as a factor in insect decline. This state Bavarian authority officially documents the connection.
claims.finding: Light pollution is a significant factor in insect decline. The study analyzes all relevant types of lighting in urban and rural spaces. Billboards are explicitly identified as a relevant light source.

claims.title: Hamburg citizens' initiative against outdoor advertising: Constitutional Court declares initiative admissible (2024)
claims.institution: World Without Fossil Ads / Adfree Cities
claims.summary: Since 2024, a popular initiative (Hamburg Werbefrei — Hamburg Ad-Free) has been underway in Hamburg to restrict outdoor advertising, in particular digital advertising screens. The Hamburg Constitutional Court (Hamburgisches Verfassungsgericht) declared the initiative legally admissible in September 2024.
claims.finding: The Hamburg Constitutional Court ruled that the initiative "Hamburg Werbefrei" (Hamburg Ad-Free) is constitutionally permissible. Around 400 activists collected over 50,000 signatures in 3 weeks (target: 80,000 = 5% of eligible voters, required for a binding referendum — Volksentscheid). The initiative calls for a ban on digital advertising screens and a reduction in poster advertising on grounds of environmental, public health, and urban landscape protection.

claims.title: Germany was the last EU country without an outdoor tobacco advertising ban — ban only took effect 2022–2024
claims.institution: The Local / Tobacco Control Laws Germany
claims.summary: Germany was the last EU member state to ban outdoor tobacco advertising. The ban was introduced in stages: tobacco products from January 2022, heated tobacco products from January 2023, and e-cigarettes from January 2024.
claims.finding: The tobacco industry spent approximately 100 million euros per year on street and cinema advertising in Germany. For decades Germany was a special case within the EU: while other member states had long since banned outdoor tobacco advertising, Germany's politically influential tobacco industry blocked the prohibition. The ban only came following significant public and EU pressure.

claims.title: São Paulo: total outdoor advertising ban (2007) — 70% public support after 5 years
claims.summary: São Paulo introduced the "Lei Cidade Limpa" (Clean City Law) in 2007 — the most comprehensive outdoor advertising ban in the world. 15,000 billboards were removed, digital screens banned, advertising on buses prohibited, and 300,000 non-compliant business signs taken down.
claims.finding: A survey in 2011 (4 years after the ban) showed that 70% of São Paulo's 11 million residents regarded the ban positively. Unexpected consequences: the ban revealed historic architecture that had previously been obscured by advertising, and it stimulated street art. Clear Channel challenged the law in court — and lost.

claims.title: Grenoble: Europe's first ad-free city district (2015) — 326 billboards replaced with trees
claims.summary: Grenoble (France) became the first European city to introduce a comprehensive outdoor advertising ban in its urban area in 2015. Mayor Éric Piolle (Greens) terminated the city's billboard contract and had 326 advertising panels (including 64 large billboards) removed.
claims.finding: 2,051 square metres of advertising space were eliminated. As a replacement: 300+ new community notice boards (Bürgertafeln) for non-profit announcements, trees, and open spaces for local cultural groups. Financial loss: 600,000 euros per year in advertising revenue. The model demonstrates that cities can forgo advertising revenue and reclaim public space.

claims.title: EU food industry self-commitment on children's advertising: 85% of products fail to meet WHO criteria
claims.summary: Analysis by the European consumer organisation BEUC (Bureau Européen des Unions de Consommateurs) of the EU Pledge — the food industry's voluntary commitment not to advertise unhealthy products to children. Conclusion: total failure of self-regulation.
claims.finding: 21 companies responsible for over 80% of European food advertising expenditure have signed up to the EU Pledge. Nevertheless, 85% of the products these companies market to children would be prohibited from advertising under WHO nutritional criteria. Voluntary self-regulatory commitments are ineffective.

claims.title: Deutscher Werberat: self-regulation without consumer representation and without enforcement authority
claims.summary: Academic analysis of the structural weaknesses of German advertising self-regulation (Deutscher Werberat — German Advertising Standards Council). Documents structural deficiencies that prevent effective consumer protection.
claims.finding: The Deutscher Werberat (German Advertising Standards Council) has no consumer representation on its board — only a liaison committee. It can demand voluntary compliance but has no binding enforcement powers. Advertising practices can continue unimpeded while proceedings are in progress. In 2023 the Council issued only 8 formal reprimands (Rügen) despite thousands of advertisements in circulation.

claims.title: BNatSchG § 41a: Germany enshrines light emission protection in nature conservation law — implementation 2027
claims.summary: In 2021, §41a was inserted into the Bundesnaturschutzgesetz (BNatSchG — Federal Nature Conservation Act), providing for protection against light emissions. The provision is not yet in force — it requires an implementing ordinance (Durchführungsverordnung) announced for 2027 as part of the national biodiversity strategy.
claims.finding: The German legislature has officially recognised light pollution as a nature conservation problem and incorporated it into the Federal Nature Conservation Act. Illuminated advertising panels and digital DOOH screens in Germany are in urban areas almost twice as numerous as street lamps, and contribute substantially to light pollution.

claims.title: One large digital advertising display consumes as much electricity as 11 households per year (41,627 kWh)
claims.summary: Adfree Cities UK measured the electricity consumption of various types of digital out-of-home advertising displays and compared them with household electricity usage.
claims.finding: A large digital advertising display (6.4 m × 3.1 m) consumes **41,627 kWh per year** — equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of 11 British households. A medium-sized display (1.2 m × 1.8 m, "Six Sheet") consumes 11,501 kWh/year (3 households). A double-sided unit in a city center consumes as much as 4 households. At night (10 pm–6 am), one large display consumes as much as 8.5 households during the same period.

claims.title: Advertising screens in Leeds consume 4.1 GWh/year — equivalent to 3,300 residents
claims.summary: A city-wide measurement of the electricity consumption of digital advertising screens in Leeds (UK) by Adfree Cities. Compared with the electricity consumption of the city's population.
claims.finding: The digital advertising screens in Leeds consume a total of **4.1 GWh per year** — enough to power 3,300 residents. This is the measured electricity consumption solely for commercial out-of-home advertising in a medium-sized British city.

claims.title: Germany switched off digital advertising screens at night in 2022 — due to the energy crisis
claims.summary: During the energy crisis of 2022 (triggered by Russia's halt of gas supplies), Germany, together with Austria, Spain and France, mandated that digital advertising screens be switched off between 10 pm and 6 am. Berlin's Kurfürstendamm (a major commercial boulevard) and other high-visibility advertising sites went dark at night.
claims.finding: During the 2022 energy crisis, digital advertising displays in several EU countries were classified as non-essential energy consumers and shut down at night. This constitutes an explicit government acknowledgement that outdoor advertising ranks below essential energy consumers.

claims.title: 600,000 tonnes of PVC advertising banner waste per year in the US alone
claims.summary: Data from the EU-funded ECOBOARD project (CORDIS) and EnKad Sciences on the volume of waste generated by advertising banners and billboards.
claims.finding: In the United States alone, **600,000 tonnes of PVC advertising banner waste** are disposed of annually. In the Brussels region, 10,000 billboards generate **68,000 m² (approx. 680 tonnes) of vinyl waste** per year. Across Europe, more than **6 million m² of poster paper** is discarded — not recycled — **every 2 weeks**, containing environmentally harmful printing inks and toxic adhesives.

claims.title: PVC advertising banners: toxic across their entire lifecycle — 1,000-year decomposition time
claims.summary: Greenpeace analysis of the toxicity of PVC (polyvinyl chloride) across its entire lifecycle. PVC is the material used in the vast majority of all outdoor advertising banners and poster backings.
claims.finding: PVC causes environmental and health damage at every stage: **Production** (PVC consumes 30–40% of all industrially produced chlorine; generates dioxins), **Use** (plasticizers/phthalates leach out and damage the hormonal system, reproduction, and respiratory tract), and **Disposal** (release of dioxins during incineration; 1,000+ years decomposition time in landfills). Phthalates from PVC are detected in waterways, air, and human tissue.

claims.title: Inks for outdoor advertising: toluene, heavy metals (Cd, Pb), BPA — massive VOC emissions
claims.summary: Scientific analysis of the chemical ingredients in printing inks used for large-format printing (as used for outdoor advertising and billboards). Printing inks are an often-overlooked component of the environmental costs of outdoor advertising.
claims.finding: Printing inks used for advertising contain as their primary solvents **toluene (approx. 70% of all emitted chemicals)**, as well as methyl ethyl ketone, xylene, and 1,1,1-trichloroethane — all volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and hazardous air pollutants (HAPs). Additionally: **cadmium, lead** (heavy metals), **bisphenol A (BPA)** (an endocrine disruptor), and synthetic antioxidants.

claims.title: Warsaw residents would pay up to €9.3 million/year to reduce outdoor advertising
claims.summary: A peer-reviewed study assessing the external costs of outdoor advertising in Warsaw (Poland) by measuring residents' willingness to pay for a reduction in advertising.
claims.finding:
Warsaw residents were willing to pay:
- **€1.7–4.1 million/year** for a reduction in freestanding advertising structures
- **€5.5–9.3 million/year** for a reduction in building-mounted advertising
- An average of **€15–23 per person per year** for advertising reduction

These figures quantify the external costs of outdoor advertising that are currently borne entirely by the public and not compensated by the advertising industry.

claims.title: Attention interruptions from advertising destroy up to 40% of productive working time
claims.summary: An economic analysis of the attention economy as an external cost factor. Examines whether a Pigouvian tax on attention capture by advertising is justified.
claims.finding: According to APA (American Psychological Association) research, attention interruptions from advertising and other distractions destroy up to **40% of productive working time**. Multitasking and forced attention-switching deplete neural glucose reserves disproportionately. The authors propose a Pigouvian tax on attention capture — analogous to environmental taxes — because the cognitive costs are fully externalized: advertisers profit while those affected bear the costs.

claims.title: Manufacturing a digital billboard: 3.5 times larger CO₂ footprint than a traditional one
claims.institution: GenOptic Smart Displays / LED Sign Supply (industry-independent technical analysis)
claims.summary: Technical lifecycle analysis of digital LED billboards compared with traditional static billboards. Assesses manufacturing and operational emissions.
claims.finding: The **manufacture of a digital billboard** generates a **3.5 times larger CO₂ footprint** than the manufacture of a traditional static billboard. LED displays over 10 years can, however, save 18 tonnes of CO₂ in operation compared with LCD screens. The manufacturing phase alone means: every new digital billboard represents a substantial CO₂ investment that takes years to amortize.

claims.title: Outdoor advertising is dominated by a few global 'big players' (JCDecaux, Clear Channel, Ströer)
claims.summary: The outdoor advertising market is heavily monopolized. A small number of large corporations (JCDecaux, Clear Channel, Ströer, Wall GmbH, Outfront Media) control the majority of advertising spaces in public areas worldwide.
claims.finding: This oligopoly position enables these corporations to exert enormous political and economic pressure on municipalities (local governments). Local and small businesses can often not afford advertising space in city centers, meaning that public space primarily carries messages from global brands.

claims.title: Municipalities privatize public space through 'bus shelter contracts'
claims.summary: Cities increasingly no longer finance public infrastructure (such as bus shelters and public toilets) from tax revenues, but instead hand over their provision to advertising corporations in exchange for long-term advertising rights.
claims.finding: These contracts, often concluded for 10 to 15 years, bind municipalities to the advertising industry over the long term. They make it legally difficult or impossible for cities to subsequently regulate or ban outdoor advertising for climate protection or health reasons. JCDecaux and Ströer are pioneers in this model.

claims.title: Lobbying by outdoor advertisers blocks stricter light protection and advertising ban legislation
claims.summary: The advertising industry invests considerable sums in lobbying at the municipal and national level to prevent or weaken regulations on DOOH (Digital Out of Home) screens.
claims.finding: Reports from NGOs such as Corporate Europe Observatory show that outdoor advertisers systematically exert pressure to obtain exemptions from light emission laws (e.g., mandatory shutdown at night) and restrictions on advertising for unhealthy products. The argument frequently made is the alleged financial dependence of municipalities on advertising revenues.

claims.title: Digital billboards significantly increase accident risk through visual distraction
claims.summary: A comprehensive collection of studies by Scenic America shows that digital billboards (DOOH) divert drivers' gaze from the road significantly longer than static signs.
claims.finding: A glance away from the road lasting more than two seconds — which is frequently triggered by changing or animated digital content — dramatically increases the risk of an accident. Studies conducted in the United States (including in Alabama and Florida) document elevated crash rates in the immediate vicinity of such installations.

claims.title: Methodological flaws in industry-funded safety studies on digital billboards
claims.summary: The advertising industry frequently cites studies (such as the 2013 FHWA study) to claim that digital billboards are traffic-safe. Independent reviews, however, reveal serious methodological flaws in these industry-supported investigations.
claims.finding: Independent traffic safety experts (such as Jerry Wachtel) demonstrate that exculpatory studies often suffer from excessively small sample sizes, inadequate measuring instruments, and flawed experimental designs. Independent data consistently shows an elevated risk of cognitive and visual distraction.

claims.title: Advertising for SUVs and fossil fuel products blocks climate targets ('Upselling Smoke')
claims.summary: The 'Badvertising' campaign documents that advertising for high-emission products (such as SUVs and short-haul flights) directly benefits sales figures and thus CO₂ emissions, drawing parallels to tobacco advertising.
claims.finding: Despite massive efforts toward climate protection, outdoor advertising actively drives the sale of particularly climate-damaging SUVs. The report argues that a transport transition (shift away from car dependency) is impossible as long as public space is used to promote the most harmful modes of transport.

claims.title: Outdoor advertising is disproportionately concentrated in low-income neighborhoods ('Unavoidable Impact')
claims.summary: A comprehensive study in the United Kingdom shows that commercial outdoor advertising appears up to six times more frequently in low-income areas than in affluent neighborhoods.
claims.finding: The report "Unavoidable Impact" documents that people in poorer neighborhoods are not only more frequently exposed to advertising for junk food, alcohol, and gambling, but also suffer more severely from visual pollution and light pollution (DOOH). Affluent residential areas often successfully repel advertising billboards.

claims.title: LANUV NRW Technical Report 113: commercial outdoor lighting drives regional light pollution
claims.institution: Landesamt für Natur, Umwelt und Verbraucherschutz NRW (LANUV)
claims.summary: The Landesamt für Natur, Umwelt und Verbraucherschutz NRW (LANUV) (State Office for Nature, Environment and Consumer Protection of North Rhine-Westphalia) conducted a state-wide survey of sky glow in NRW. Commercial outdoor lighting and illuminated advertising are identified as significant emission factors.
claims.finding: The technical report and the associated guidelines (the 'Licht-Erlass' NRW, i.e., the NRW Light Ordinance) show that artificial outdoor lighting — including intensely luminous DOOH installations — contributes to massive disruptions of human biorhythms and to insect decline. The authority recommends strict limits on luminance levels and nighttime switch-offs to reduce emissions.

claims.title: Cologne-based advertising group Ströer secures monopoly position in NRW municipalities through lobbying
claims.summary: The Cologne (NRW)-based outdoor advertising giant Ströer SE & Co. KGaA uses its financial power and direct political lobbying to secure exclusive, long-term concessions for advertising space on public land.
claims.finding: Investigations by investigative NGOs such as Correctiv show that the company's market power is so great that cities effectively have no real alternatives when awarding street furniture contracts (bus shelters). Ströer is also officially registered in the Lobbyregister (the federal lobbying register) and exerts direct influence on urban development policy matters and data protection guidelines.

claims.title: Citizens' initiatives in NRW demand restrictive building codes against digital billboards
claims.summary: In several large cities in North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW) — particularly Cologne (Köln), the home city of Ströer, and Münster — civil society initiatives have formed that are calling for a ban or strong restrictions on commercial outdoor advertising.
claims.finding: These initiatives aim to amend local building regulations (Bauordnung) so that digital advertising installations (DOOH) and alternating illuminated signs in public spaces are prohibited. They argue on grounds of visual noise (visueller Lärm), unnecessary energy consumption during the climate crisis, and the commercialisation of cities.

claims.title: DOOH screens covertly capture biometric data for audience analysis
claims.summary: Modern digital advertising screens (DOOH) are increasingly equipped with cameras and sensors that capture biometric data and movement profiles of passers-by in order to deliver targeted advertising ("programmatic") to specific audience segments.
claims.finding: Investigations by NGOs show that companies use technologies for Automated Facial Detection (AFD) as well as Wi-Fi sniffing to analyze the age, gender, mood, and dwell time of individuals in front of screens. This occurs in public space, usually without the active consent (opt-in) of those affected, raising serious data protection and ethical concerns.

claims.title: Sweden bans digital billboards on rural roads following study by the Transport Administration
claims.summary: A detailed field study by the Swedish Transport Administration (Trafikverket) demonstrated that digital billboards significantly distract drivers. As a direct consequence, the Swedish government ordered the removal of the billboards.
claims.finding: The study found that drivers averted their gaze from the road significantly longer at DOOH installations (often exceeding 2 seconds) compared with static signs. Since gaze diversions exceeding 2 seconds are considered highly dangerous, the government decided that the economic interests of operators must be subordinated to the protection of traffic safety. The pilot program for approving such billboards was subsequently terminated.

claims.title: Gambling and sports betting advertising in public space normalizes addictive behavior
claims.summary: The omnipresence of sports betting and gambling advertising at bus stops and on billboards is identified by public health experts as a major driver of addictive behavior.
claims.finding: Outdoor advertising for gambling normalizes risky behavior, triggers relapse in recovered problem gamblers, and introduces adolescents to sports betting at an early age. Unlike TV advertising, vulnerable individuals cannot avoid advertising in public space — for example, on the way to school or work.

claims.title: A double-sided digital billboard consumes the annual electricity equivalent of 3 to 4 average households
claims.summary: Despite the shift to LED technology, the absolute energy consumption of digital billboards (DOOH) remains immensely high, as they illuminate continuously around the clock, require cooling, and emit extremely high brightness.
claims.finding: Research confirms that a typical double-sided digital advertising screen at a bus stop consumes approximately 11,000 to 14,000 kWh of electricity per year. This is equivalent to the electricity consumption of three to four average households. This massive consumption of resources takes place in the midst of a global energy and climate crisis.

claims.title: High-emissions sectors (airlines, SUVs, fast food) dominate advertising budgets for digital out-of-home
claims.summary: An analysis of advertisers using outdoor advertising shows that public space surfaces are booked disproportionately often by climate-damaging industries seeking to drive non-sustainable consumption.
claims.finding: The most profitable clients for outdoor advertising companies are automobile manufacturers (particularly SUVs), low-cost airlines, fast-food chains, and the fashion industry (Fast Fashion). The constant visual presence of these products in public space cements an extremely resource-intensive lifestyle as a social norm (induced consumption).

claims.title: Moving images on digital advertising screens compel involuntary attention ('Orienting Response')
claims.summary: The psychology behind digital screens (DOOH) is based on the exploitation of evolutionary reflexes. Unlike static posters, changing or moving images compel the human brain to look.
claims.finding: The so-called orienting response (Orientierungsreflex) is an involuntary neurological mechanism that compels people to pay attention to sudden changes in their peripheral visual field (such as changes in light or motion on a screen), since this is evolutionarily associated with danger. DOOH installations deliberately exploit this reflex to "steal" attention. One cannot decide not to look.

claims.title: Freestanding, double-sided advertising structures function as visual and physical barriers
claims.summary: The hardware design of so-called "double posters" (City-Light-Boards — freestanding double-sided advertising panels, typically found at transit stops) has far-reaching consequences for the architecture of public space, as they physically intrude into pavements and pedestrian zones.
claims.finding: While traditional posters are usually mounted flat against walls, double-sided advertising installations (often 2 to 3 metres tall) are installed freestanding and perpendicular to the direction of pedestrian flow in order to guarantee maximum visibility from both directions. Studies show that this placement narrows pavements, restricts accessibility for wheelchair users, and cuts through urban sightlines.

claims.title: Active LED screens generate many times more light pollution than backlit posters
claims.summary: The technological shift from traditional 'illuminated surfaces' (backlit paper) to digital LED screens (DOOH) represents a drastic worsening of light emissions.
claims.finding: A traditional City Light Poster (a backlit static advertising poster common in German cities) illuminates passively, with fluorescent light filtered through printed paper. A digital DOOH screen, however, consists of thousands of tiny LED lamps that emit light directly (and often non-directionally) into the surroundings. To be visible in daylight, LEDs radiate extremely brightly (up to 7,000 nits). Even in dimmed night mode, they contribute massively to sky glow (Skyglow) due to the blue-heavy LED spectrum.

claims.title: The gradual conversion of illuminated advertising surfaces to digital screens circumvents regulatory processes
claims.summary: Advertising corporations exploit gaps in municipal building and planning regulations to digitalise public spaces without renewed public participation.
claims.finding: In many municipalities, contracts or permits exist for existing "illuminated advertising installations" (e.g. analogue City Light Posters). Outdoor advertisers are increasingly using these existing permits to physically replace the paper poster with a bright DOOH LED screen ("digital upgrade"). Because the physical dimensions of the casing often remain the same, planning authorities frequently — and incorrectly — do not classify this as a new construction, thereby bypassing environmental assessments and objections from local residents.

claims.title: Ad-free cities reinvest advertising spaces into cultural funding and local art
claims.summary: The French city of Grenoble has proven that commercial outdoor advertising is not without alternatives. Instead of renewing advertising contracts, commercial surfaces were dismantled or replaced with citizen information and art.
claims.finding: In 2014, the mayor of Grenoble decided to remove 326 commercial advertising billboards from public space. Instead of the expected commercial vacuum, 50 new surfaces were created for local cultural and social announcements. The city planted trees at the former advertising sites. The loss in advertising revenue (approx. 600,000 euros) was offset by cuts to the mayor's representation budget and by the positive effects of the improved quality of life.

claims.title: Financing public transit infrastructure through levies rather than advertising corporations
claims.summary: The argument that outdoor advertising is necessary to fund bus and tram stops is structurally flawed. There are more sustainable, advertising-free financing models.
claims.finding: Cities frequently exchange the provision of bus shelters for extensive advertising rights (Public-Private Partnerships). However, analyses show that the indirect costs — electricity consumption of the displays, traffic distraction, induced CO2 emissions — often outweigh the apparent financial benefit. Alternatively, cities like São Paulo (following the advertising ban "Cidade Limpa") finance their infrastructure through redistributed levies, taxes on vacant properties, or municipal self-financing, thereby retaining full control over the design and energy consumption of their street furniture.

claims.title: Advertising corporations systematically ignore building regulations and brightness limits
claims.summary: The installation and operation of digital billboards frequently violates local building regulations. Corporations exploit the overloaded capacity of municipal authorities.
claims.finding: Investigations in the United Kingdom reveal systematic disregard for conditions and requirements. DOOH installations are often erected entirely without planning permission. Even where conditions exist, contractually agreed brightness limits (luminance) are exceeded, or mandatory night-time switch-offs (e.g. from 23:00 to 06:00) are simply ignored. Advertising corporations often accept fines as a "cost of doing business", since revenue from the illegal advertising airtime is higher, and municipal planning departments are too understaffed to pursue Discontinuance Notices through the courts.

claims.title: British municipalities issue strict advertising bans for high-emissions products
claims.summary: A growing number of municipal and regional governments are using their role as landowners to ban advertising for high-emission products on civic infrastructure.
claims.finding: Cities including Edinburgh, Sheffield, Cambridgeshire, and Somerset have introduced legally binding clauses into their advertising policies. These prohibit advertising corporations (such as JCDecaux or Clear Channel) from displaying advertising for flights, fossil-fuel-powered SUVs, and fossil fuels on municipal land (e.g. bus shelters, council-owned hoardings). The municipalities argue that promoting these products is in direct contradiction to their urban climate protection targets ("Net Zero").

claims.title: The Swiss Federal Supreme Court confirms the legality of municipal advertising bans
claims.summary: The legal assumption that a complete ban on outdoor advertising constitutes an impermissible interference with economic freedom (Wirtschaftsfreiheit) has been refuted by Switzerland's highest court.
claims.finding: The municipality of Vernier (Canton of Geneva) resolved to ban commercial poster advertising throughout its territory in order to protect the visual landscape and reduce visual environmental pollution. Advertising corporations (including APG SGA) challenged the ban through every level of the court system. In 2024, the Swiss Federal Supreme Court (Bundesgericht) issued a final ruling in favour of the municipality: the ban is lawful. The court found that the public interest in an intact local environment and in protecting residents from unsolicited consumer pressure outweighs the purely commercial interests of the advertising industry.

claims.title: The advertising industry's self-regulation is structurally inadequate and reactive
claims.summary: Bodies of "voluntary self-regulation" (such as the Werberat — Advertising Standards Council — in Germany, or the ASA — Advertising Standards Authority — in the UK) are unable to effectively prevent harmful outdoor advertising.
claims.finding: The advertising industry's self-regulatory systems share a structural design flaw: they operate almost exclusively reactively. There is no pre-clearance process for posters. This means that severely harmful or misleading advertising is first displayed and forced upon the public (including children). By the time complaints are submitted, reviewed, and formal reprimands issued, the typical one-to-two-week booking period for the poster has in any case already expired. The harm has already occurred.

claims.title: Four US states have completely banned outdoor advertising to protect their economies and tourism
claims.summary: A strict ban on outdoor advertising is not an economic disadvantage but a tangible economic competitive advantage — as four US states demonstrate.
claims.finding: In the United States, the four states of Hawaii, Maine, Vermont, and Alaska have banned outdoor advertising across their entire territories by law. Contrary to the advertising industry's claim that bans harm local economies, the governments of these states argue the opposite: protecting the landscape ("Scenic Beauty") from visual pollution ("Billboard Blight") is a decisive factor in promoting tourism and quality of life. Preserving an unobstructed landscape is economically more valuable than advertising revenue.

claims.title: Billboards in residential areas significantly lower adjacent property values
claims.summary: Visual pollution from outdoor advertising does not merely harm aesthetics, but has directly measurable negative economic impacts on residents.
claims.finding: Analyses of the US real estate market show that close proximity to commercial billboards (so-called "billboard blight") significantly reduces the value of adjacent residential properties. The contributing factors include light pollution from illumination or digital LEDs, the destruction of sightlines, and the psychological association of billboards with neglect and pure commercialization. This is particularly problematic because billboards have historically been concentrated disproportionately in already low-income neighborhoods (a pattern linked to "redlining" — the discriminatory practice of denying services to residents in minority neighborhoods).

claims.title: Metropolises temporarily replace commercial billboards with city-wide art exhibitions
claims.summary: The infrastructure of outdoor advertising can be repurposed subversively. A project in Tehran demonstrated the enormous social and psychological healing effect of art in place of consumer pressure.
claims.finding: In May 2015, the mayor of Tehran (Iran) ordered that all approximately 1,500 commercial advertising billboards in the metropolis be pasted over for ten days as part of the project "A Gallery as Big as a Town." Instead of advertisements for smartphones and detergents, the billboards suddenly displayed works by Picasso, Matisse, Munch, and traditional Persian art. The experiment demonstrated impressively that the logistical infrastructure of the advertising industry can be used to transform a city into a giant open-air gallery and provide citizens with genuine cultural added value.

claims.title: Civil society 'adblock' networks block hundreds of new permit applications annually
claims.summary: Citizens are increasingly and successfully pushing back against the privatization of public space by outdoor advertising, by strategically using planning and building regulations.
claims.finding: Local grassroots organizations (such as the Adblock network in the UK or Résistance à l'Agression Publicitaire (Resistance to Advertising Aggression) in France) systematically monitor municipal planning portals for new applications for DOOH screens and billboards. By mobilizing large numbers of residents and submitting well-founded objections (based on traffic safety, light pollution, and heritage protection), these groups regularly force advertising corporations to withdraw planning applications, or secure rejections from urban planning authorities.

claims.title: Legislative proposals from civil society: the 'Berlin Werbefrei' initiative
claims.summary: The commercialization of public space is encountering massive democratic resistance in Germany, which has manifested in formal legislative procedures.
claims.finding: The citizens' initiative "Berlin Werbefrei" (Berlin Ad-Free) collected over 36,000 valid signatures in the first stage of a Volksbegehren (citizens' referendum process) in order to introduce its own far-reaching legislative draft into the Berlin Abgeordnetenhaus (state parliament). The draft envisions radically banning product and consumer advertising in Berlin's public space. Only advertising at the point of sale (e.g., the sign above a bakery), event announcements, and public interest information would remain permitted.

claims.title: The French Climate Law (Loi Climat) bans fossil fuel advertising and strengthens local DOOH prohibitions
claims.summary: The French government has enacted landmark climate and advertising legislation at the national level that directly affects the business models of OOH (out-of-home) and DOOH (digital out-of-home) operators.
claims.finding: The "Loi Climat et Résilience" (Climate and Resilience Act), which entered into force in August 2022, bans advertising for fossil fuels (gas, coal, oil) nationwide. Additionally, this law now formally grants mayors and local authorities ("Maires") executive policing powers (Pouvoir de Police — executive enforcement authority) to strictly restrict or completely remove digital and illuminated advertising panels within their municipal area by local decree. Previously, this decision-making authority often resided at uncertain intermediate national-regional levels.

claims.title: Digital screens in Germany conflict with strict requirements on insect and emissions protection
claims.summary: The expansion of Digital Out-of-Home (DOOH) is increasingly running up against the hard limits of national environmental and nature conservation law in Germany.
claims.finding: In Germany, the Lichtimmissionsrichtlinie (LAI) (Light Emission Guideline), based on the Bundes-Immissionsschutzgesetz (BImSchG) (Federal Immission Control Act), stipulates strict limit values for harmful environmental effects caused by light. DOOH screens, which can reach up to 10,000 nits of brightness, frequently exceed these tolerance values with regard to glare effects on traffic and 'room brightening' in bedrooms. Furthermore, the new German Insektenschutzgesetz (Insect Protection Act) and amendments to the Bundesnaturschutzgesetz BNatSchG (Federal Nature Conservation Act) prohibit the installation of lighting systems in certain nature conservation areas and mandate massively reduced light emissions at night, as artificial LED light (particularly in the blue spectrum emitted by DOOH) decimates nocturnal insect populations (the 'vacuum cleaner effect').

claims.title: The 'Path-to-Purchase' match: passive tracking of mobile IDs by DOOH kiosks
claims.summary: The linking of physical advertising locations with digital identity markers enables seamless tracking of citizens in public space.
claims.finding: Modern DOOH kiosks (Digital-Out-of-Home) frequently use Wi-Fi and Bluetooth sensors to passively capture the unique MAC addresses or mobile advertising IDs of passers-by. This data is cross-referenced with location data from apps and third-party providers to measure the so-called "path-to-purchase": tracking whether a person who passed a poster later enters the advertised store or searches for the product online. NGOs such as Big Brother Watch criticize that this cross-referencing occurs without the informed consent of citizens and transforms public space into a private surveillance network.

claims.title: Disruption of the circadian rhythm by high-intensity blue LED light from DOOH screens
claims.summary: Nighttime illumination from digital advertising displays directly interferes with the hormonal regulation of the human sleep-wake cycle.
claims.finding: Digital advertising screens use LEDs that often operate at very high color temperatures (above 6,500 Kelvin), which emit a high proportion of blue light. This short-wave light suppresses the release of melatonin in the pineal gland — a hormone essential for sleep and cellular regeneration. Residents in urban areas whose windows are lit up by DOOH (Digital Out-of-Home) screens suffer from a chronic shift in their circadian rhythm. The American Medical Association (AMA) warns of long-term consequences such as sleep disorders, metabolic diseases, and an increased risk of certain cancers caused by ALAN (Artificial Light at Night).

claims.title: The hidden e-waste cycle: short lifespan and resource consumption of DOOH hardware
claims.summary: The 'digitalization' of outdoor advertising generates enormous quantities of difficult-to-recycle electronic waste (e-waste) and consumes critical raw materials.
claims.finding: Unlike analogue billboards, which can last for decades, digital LED screens have a short technical and economic lifespan of often only 5 to 8 years. Rapid technological progress and LED degradation lead to frequent 'hardware upgrades.' This generates tonnes of e-waste containing rare earth elements, lead, and cadmium. Studies show that recycling these complex electronic components is extremely energy-intensive, and disposal often takes place in countries of the Global South under precarious conditions, causing severe soil and water contamination.

claims.title: Physical invasion of private space through light trespass (Light Trespass)
claims.summary: Digital Out-of-Home (DOOH) installations violate the boundaries of private space by emitting unsolicited light into homes and bedrooms.
claims.finding: In urban planning, the phenomenon of "light trespass" (Lichteinbruch — the unwanted intrusion of light into private spaces) is regarded as a form of spatial boundary violation. DOOH screens often emit light in an undirected manner, illuminating the facades and interiors of nearby residents as if it were daylight. Because the light is commercial and often dynamic (changing images, flashing), it is psychologically harder to ignore than static street lighting. Affected residents report a massive reduction in quality of life and the feeling that, even within their own four walls, they can no longer escape the pressure of advertising.

claims.title: Screens that look back: real-time analysis of passersby through Anonymized Video Analytics (AVA)
claims.summary: Modern advertising screens are equipped with sensors that scan the audience in real time in order to psychologically optimize advertising messages.
claims.finding: An increasing number of DOOH installations integrate camera systems that capture the faces of passers-by using "Anonymized Video Analytics" (AVA). The technology analyzes in fractions of a second the age, gender, dwell time, and in some cases even the emotional reaction (mood) to the displayed advertising. Although the industry claims not to store images, the analysis occurs without the knowledge or consent of passers-by. This "eye tracking" in public space is used to perfect the effectiveness of manipulation techniques and to systematically undermine the cognitive defenses of citizens.

claims.title: Hardware dumping: export of outdated and energy-intensive advertising infrastructure to the Global South
claims.summary: The modernization of advertising infrastructure in the Global North leads to the export of ecologically harmful and inefficient hardware to developing countries.
claims.finding: When advertising companies in Europe or North America upgrade their inventory to the latest, more energy-efficient LED generation, the old, power-hungry, and often maintenance-intensive panels are frequently exported as "second-hand hardware" to countries in the Global South. There, these installations contribute to overloading local power grids and end up on informal waste dumps at the end of their lifecycle. This phenomenon is criticized as "eco-colonialism" (the externalization of environmental costs onto less powerful nations): the Global North "cleans up" its urban footprint while the ecological and energy-related damage is offloaded to countries with weaker environmental laws.

claims.title: The municipal debt trap: long-term dependency through advertising-financed urban infrastructure
claims.institution: Corporate Europe Observatory / Municipal Finance Studies
claims.summary: Long-term advertising contracts bind municipalities to private corporations and curtail democratic authority over the design of public space.
claims.finding: Cities frequently enter into contracts lasting 15 to 20 years with advertising companies, in which the provision of bus shelters or public toilets is exchanged for exclusive advertising rights. These Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) often develop into debt traps: municipalities lose control over the cityscape and can often only enforce new ecological or social standards (e.g. bans on junk food advertising) by making massive compensation payments to the companies. Furthermore, the locations of the infrastructure often prioritise advertising visibility rather than the needs of citizens, leading to neglect of outlying districts.

claims.title: Signal masking: DOOH impairs visibility of emergency and traffic signals
claims.summary: The extreme luminance of digital billboards can impede the perception of critical traffic signals and emergency vehicles.
claims.finding: It is well established in the psychology of visual perception that stronger light stimuli can mask weaker ones. High-power LED screens positioned in the line of sight to traffic signals or road signs can drastically reduce their signal effectiveness, particularly at night or in poor weather conditions (rain, fog). Furthermore, the enormous brightness and color dynamics of DOOH installations can cause the flashing warning lights of approaching emergency vehicles (blue light) to be lost in the visual noise of the surroundings, or to be perceived too late — dangerously extending the reaction time of road users.

claims.title: Displacement of local culture: the commercialization of spaces for community art and murals
claims.institution: Urban Sociology Review / Culture Action Europe
claims.summary: The aggressive expansion of commercial advertising space is depriving the local arts scene and civic movements of the physical space for non-commercial forms of expression.
claims.finding: In many major cities, facades that were previously free or used for community murals (wall paintings) are being taken over by large-format advertising banners or digital screens. This process leads to a cultural homogenization: instead of locally rooted, political or aesthetic art, interchangeable global brand messages appear. Sociological studies show that this weakens residents' identification with their neighborhood, since public space is no longer perceived as a place for co-creation but as a pure consumption zone. The city's "canvas" is sold to the highest bidder instead of serving as a stage for local culture.

claims.title: The 'Nordic Minimalism': ad-free smart city concepts to promote quality of life
claims.institution: Nordic Council of Ministers / Urban Planning Case Studies
claims.summary: Some Scandinavian cities demonstrate that modern urban development ("Smart City") is more successful without the visual and psychological burden of outdoor advertising.
claims.finding: In various urban development projects across Scandinavia (e.g. in districts of Oslo or Stockholm), a "Human-Centric" approach is pursued that prioritises the reduction of visual noise. When planning connected infrastructure (smart lamp posts, information kiosks), the integration of advertising displays is deliberately avoided. Instead, these surfaces are used for real-time citizen information, climate data, or simple greenery. Studies show that citizens in these advertising-free spaces experience a greater sense of security, less stress, and stronger social cohesion, which increases the long-term attractiveness of the location.

claims.title: Amsterdam and Haarlem ban advertising for meat and fossil fuel products in public space
claims.summary: Dutch cities are using their control over public space to actively reduce consumption of climate-damaging products.
claims.finding: As the first capital city in the world, Amsterdam passed a law in 2026 prohibiting advertising for meat products and fossil fuels (cars, flights, oil) at municipal advertising sites (bus shelters, railway stations). Haarlem pioneered this movement in 2022. The aim is to support the cities' climate targets by ending the visual normalisation of products with a high carbon footprint. The cities argue that providing public space for the promotion of climate-damaging products is in direct contradiction to the public interest mandate.

claims.title: London's junk food advertising ban is estimated to prevent 95,000 obesity cases
claims.institution: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM)
claims.summary: Scientific studies document the massive positive effect of advertising restrictions on public health.
claims.finding: A comprehensive study by LSHTM (London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine) and the University of Sheffield examined the 2019 ban on advertising for products high in fat, sugar, and salt (HFSS — High in Fat, Sugar and Salt) across the London transport network (TfL — Transport for London). The result: the ban led to a reduction in weekly energy intake from HFSS products of an average of 6.7% per household. This corresponds to a long-term prevention of an estimated 94,867 obesity cases and nearly 3,000 cases of type 2 diabetes in London. In addition, the British health system (NHS) is saving costs exceeding £200 million as a result.

claims.title: France bans large commercial billboards in municipalities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants
claims.summary: French environmental law actively protects rural areas and smaller municipalities from the visual flooding of commercial advertising.
claims.finding: As part of a comprehensive reform of advertising law, France enacted legislation in 2010 that has been fully applicable since July 2015: in all municipalities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants (that are not part of a larger metropolitan area), large-format commercial outdoor billboard advertising is fundamentally prohibited. Permitted only are specific directional signs for local cultural activities, regional products, or essential services. Violations expose advertisers to daily fines.

claims.title: Strict statutory advertising bans near schools to protect minors from consumer pressure
claims.institution: Ministerium für Schule und Bildung NRW
claims.summary: In Germany, the school is legally enshrined as an advertising-free protected space in order to preserve pedagogical integrity and pupils' independence.
claims.finding: As a representative example, § 99 of the Schulgesetz NRW (School Act for the State of North Rhine-Westphalia) stipulates that advertising that does not serve educational purposes is generally prohibited on school premises. This encompasses both the distribution of materials and the posting of posters on school grounds. The aim is to protect minors during a sensitive phase of development from the influence of commercial actors and to ensure that school remains a place of critical reflection rather than unfiltered consumption. Sponsoring is only permitted under the strictest conditions, with the advertising effect required to "clearly take a back seat to the educational benefit."

claims.title: The concept of 'Advertised Emissions': outdoor advertising as a driver of Scope 3 emissions
claims.summary: The climate impact of the advertising industry extends far beyond the electricity consumption of screens — it lies in the induced additional consumption of CO2-intensive products.
claims.finding: Reports by Purpose Disruptors show that advertising massively increases greenhouse gas emissions from the population by artificially boosting the sale of climate-damaging products (such as SUVs, air travel, or fast food). These "Advertised Emissions" account for a significant share of the ecological footprint of an urban society. Estimates for the UK market show that the additional demand generated by advertising increases emissions by approximately 32%. Outdoor advertising acts here as a "Choice Architect" that normalises climate-damaging lifestyles in public space.

claims.title: Cities use 'amenity' rules to halt the concentration of digital screens in disadvantaged neighborhoods
claims.summary: Planning law gives cities the means to limit visual clutter (Clutter) and the associated degradation of quality of life in residential neighbourhoods.
claims.finding: In Bristol (UK), the city council has tightened guidelines interpreting the concept of "amenity" (quality of life / livability) in planning law. The aim is to prevent digital advertising screens from being disproportionately concentrated in districts that already have lower environmental quality or in lower-income neighbourhoods. The city argues that an excessive density of DOOH installations degrades the appearance of a neighbourhood, creates light pollution for residents, and violates the right to an ad-free, peaceful public space.

claims.title: Light pollution from DOOH disorients migratory birds over European cities
claims.summary: The extreme brightness of digital advertising installations at night disrupts the biological rhythms and migration routes of protected bird species.
claims.finding: Scientific studies in Europe show that large-format, high-brightness LED screens (particularly those with a high blue-light component) contribute to 'Skyglow' during nighttime hours, which disorients migratory birds. Birds are attracted to the light sources (phototaxis), leading to fatal collisions with buildings or to exhaustion caused by unnecessary detours. Since many European metropolises lie along major migration routes, the unfiltered light emission from DOOH poses a direct threat to biodiversity and undermines urban efforts for species conservation.

claims.title: Advertising promotes materialism in children and destroys intrinsic values over the long term
claims.institution: Journal of Advertising / American Academy of Advertising
claims.summary: Peer-reviewed analysis of the long-term consequences of advertising exposure on children: advertising instills materialistic values that are in direct conflict with prosocial behavior, intrinsic motivation, and psychological resilience.
claims.finding: Children who are intensively exposed to advertising demonstrably develop stronger materialistic attitudes — the equation of possessions with happiness, status, and identity. This correlates with lower self-esteem, increased dissatisfaction, and reduced life satisfaction in adulthood. Outdoor advertising in public space is particularly effective at producing this conditioning, as it represents a permanent, non-consent-based exposure.

claims.title: Outdoor alcohol advertising demonstrably increases alcohol consumption among adolescents
claims.institution: Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs
claims.summary: Peer-reviewed longitudinal study examining the relationship between the density of outdoor alcohol advertising near schools and alcohol consumption as well as consumption intentions among adolescents.
claims.finding: Adolescents in neighborhoods with a high density of outdoor alcohol advertising show significantly higher intentions to consume alcohol and report higher actual consumption. Outdoor alcohol advertising near schools and residential areas acts as an independent risk factor — more potent than TV advertising, because it cannot be avoided.

claims.title: Microplastics from PVC advertising banners contaminate soils and waterways in urban areas
claims.summary: PVC advertising banner materials — the standard material for large-format advertising — weather under UV radiation and mechanical abrasion into microplastic particles that enter soils, drainage systems, and waterways. In urban areas with a high density of OOH (out-of-home) advertising, this input pathway is significant.
claims.finding: PVC advertising banners (standard advertising material) contain plasticizers such as DEHP (endocrine-disrupting) and stabilizers such as lead and cadmium. UV weathering produces microplastic particles < 5mm that enter urban stormwater runoff. Urban stormwater runoff transports microplastics directly into waterways — wastewater treatment filters out less than 60%.

claims.title: Programmatic DOOH targeting is structurally non-compliant with the GDPR — no valid consent possible
claims.summary: The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) has clarified that capturing personal characteristics (age, gender, emotions) through camera systems in public advertising installations without valid consent is unlawful. The programmatic DOOH business model, which is based on audience measurement, is therefore structurally incompatible with the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation, known in German as DSGVO — Datenschutz-Grundverordnung).
claims.finding: DOOH screens use camera systems for the anonymized counting and classification of passers-by (Anonymized Video Analytics / AVA). The EDPB establishes: even when no biometric templates are stored, the processing of facial and bodily characteristics for audience analysis constitutes processing of personal data pursuant to Art. 4 GDPR.
